subject: trump

brief.inclusion: The 45th and 47th president of the United States, and the central figure in the appointments, campaigns, organizations and political relationships that make up the contemporary Trump network.
brief.namesakes: No plausible namesake in the presidential record; campaign-finance records should be matched by candidate identifier rather than name.

Run the evidence, quantitative, editorial and product reviews before import.

summary: The 45th and 47th president of the United States, Donald Trump converted a family real-estate business, a licensing brand and television celebrity into control of the Republican Party and two nonconsecutive presidential victories. His first term produced a major tax law, three Supreme Court appointments, restrictive immigration policies and two impeachments, and ended with his effort to overturn the 2020 election. Returned to office in 2025, he has pursued a more centralized presidency built around executive power, tariffs, mass-removal policy and direct military action, including the 2026 war with Iran.

finance.coverage: Presidential campaign committees, leadership PACs, joint fundraising committees, allied super PACs and Trump-controlled businesses are analytically separate. events.title: Born in Queens, New York City
events.summary: Donald John Trump was the fourth of five children of Mary Anne MacLeod Trump and real-estate developer Fred Trump.

events.title: Joins the family real-estate business full time
events.summary: After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania, Trump returned to New York and entered his father's business full time.

events.title: Takes control of the family business
events.summary: Trump assumed leadership of the company founded by his grandmother and father and renamed it the Trump Organization in 1973.

events.title: Publishes Trump: The Art of the Deal
events.summary: The book extended Trump's public identity from property developer to a national brand associated with dealmaking and business success.

events.title: Stars in The Apprentice
events.summary: The NBC reality show brought Trump's business persona to a national weekly audience and made the phrase “You're fired” part of his political-era brand.

events.title: Launches first successful presidential campaign
events.summary: Trump announced his Republican candidacy at Trump Tower, joining opposition to immigration and trade policy to the Make America Great Again slogan.

events.title: Wins the presidency
events.summary: Trump defeated Hillary Clinton in the Electoral College, 304 to 227, while receiving fewer popular votes nationally.

events.title: Becomes the 45th president
events.summary: Trump entered office without prior government service or military leadership, the first president to do so.

events.title: Impeached for the first time
events.summary: The House impeached Trump for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress arising from his effort to press Ukraine's president to announce investigations affecting the 2020 election; the Senate acquitted him in February 2020.

events.title: Loses reelection to Joe Biden
events.summary: Biden won 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232 and led the national popular vote by about seven million.

events.title: Effort to overturn the election culminates at the Capitol
events.summary: After weeks of pressure on state and federal officials, Trump addressed supporters who then marched to the Capitol, where the electoral count was violently disrupted. The House select committee later described a multi-part effort driven by Trump to overturn the result; Trump disputed the committee's work and conclusions.

events.title: Impeached for the second time
events.summary: The House impeached Trump after the January 6 attack. The Senate acquitted him on February 13, 2021, after he had left office.

events.title: Trial court enters New York civil-fraud judgment
events.summary: A New York judge ordered Trump and other defendants to pay more than $450 million in disgorgement and pre-judgment interest and imposed business restrictions. The judgment's later appellate history remains part of this dossier's open legal pass.
events.statusNote: The cited source establishes the trial-court result; update with the complete appellate disposition before publication.

events.title: Convicted on 34 felony counts in New York
events.summary: A Manhattan jury found Trump guilty on 34 counts of falsifying business records. He said he would appeal; the complete appeal history remains an open research item.
events.statusNote: The conviction and initial sentence are verified; appellate proceedings must be brought current before publication.

events.title: Survives assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania
events.summary: A gunman fired at Trump during a campaign rally, wounding him and killing an attendee. The raised-fist image and Trump's call to “Fight” became a defining image of the campaign.

events.title: Wins a nonconsecutive second term
events.summary: Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris, winning the national popular vote and 312 electoral votes to Harris's 226.

events.title: Becomes the 47th president
events.summary: Trump began a second, nonconsecutive term and used his inaugural address to promise rapid executive action under an “America First” program.

events.title: Justice Department sues the family company over housing discrimination
events.summary: The Justice Department accused the Trump company of discriminating against Black rental applicants. The company denied wrongdoing and resolved the case through a consent decree requiring fair-housing measures.

events.title: Assembles the Commodore Hotel redevelopment
events.summary: Trump used a Hyatt partnership and a long New York City tax abatement to redevelop the bankrupt Commodore Hotel as the Grand Hyatt, establishing his Manhattan business model.

events.title: Trump Taj Mahal enters bankruptcy protection
events.summary: Heavy borrowing for the Atlantic City casino expansion produced a debt crisis; the Taj Mahal entered bankruptcy protection in 1991 and Trump Plaza Hotel followed in 1992.

events.title: Makes the false birther claim a national political cause
events.summary: Trump became a leading promoter of the false claim that President Barack Obama was not born in the United States, using television appearances and social media to question Obama's legitimacy.

events.title: Orders entry restrictions that become the travel ban
events.summary: Trump's first version of the policy restricted entry from several Muslim-majority countries. After revisions and litigation, the Supreme Court upheld the 2017 proclamation in Trump v. Hawaii in 2018.

events.title: Announces withdrawal from the Paris climate agreement
events.summary: Trump presented withdrawal as protection for American sovereignty, industry and workers and halted implementation of the U.S. commitment.

events.title: Signs the 2017 tax law
events.summary: The law permanently reduced the corporate tax rate to 21 percent and temporarily changed individual rates, deductions and credits; it was the first term's largest legislative achievement.

events.title: Zero-tolerance prosecutions drive family separations
events.summary: The administration's referral of parents for criminal prosecution sharply increased separations of children from parents at the southwest border until a court order and policy change in June.

events.title: Third Supreme Court nominee is confirmed
events.summary: The Senate's confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett followed those of Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh, giving Trump three appointments that moved the Court substantially to the right.

events.title: Special counsel completes Russia investigation
events.summary: Robert Mueller documented a Russian campaign to influence the 2016 election and numerous contacts involving Trump associates, but said the evidence was insufficient to charge a broader conspiracy; the report did not make a traditional prosecutorial judgment on obstruction by Trump.

events.title: COVID-19 becomes the defining crisis of the first term
events.summary: Trump declared a national emergency and signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act as schools, workplaces and public life shut down. By the end of his term the reported U.S. death toll had passed 400,000.

events.title: Launches Operation Warp Speed
events.summary: The federal effort supported multiple vaccine candidates and accelerated manufacturing; Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines received emergency authorization before Trump left office.

events.title: USMCA replaces NAFTA
events.summary: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement entered into force after Trump made renegotiating NAFTA a central campaign promise.

events.title: Hosts the Abraham Accords signing
events.summary: Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain signed normalization agreements at the White House, the first of several Arab-Israeli agreements negotiated during the administration.

events.title: Jury finds Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming E. Jean Carroll
events.summary: A federal civil jury awarded Carroll $5 million. The judgment survived appellate review and reached the Supreme Court docket; a separate 2024 defamation verdict awarded Carroll another $83.3 million.

events.title: Federally indicted over the 2020 election effort
events.summary: Special counsel Jack Smith charged Trump in the election case. The prosecution was dismissed after Trump's 2024 victory under the Justice Department's policy against prosecuting a sitting president, without a trial verdict.

events.title: Trump Media becomes publicly traded
events.summary: The owner of Truth Social completed its combination with Digital World Acquisition Corp. Trump's shares became a large, publicly priced component of his wealth and were later transferred to his revocable trust.

events.title: Pardons or commutes sentences for January 6 offenses
events.summary: On his first day back in office, Trump commuted fourteen named sentences, pardoned all other people convicted of offenses connected to January 6 and directed dismissal of pending indictments.

events.title: Opens second term with sweeping immigration orders
events.summary: Trump declared the southern border situation an invasion, restricted asylum access and ordered agencies not to recognize citizenship for some U.S.-born children, initiating immediate constitutional litigation.

events.title: Signs the second term's central tax-and-spending law
events.summary: The law extended major provisions of the 2017 tax law and advanced the administration's border, energy and social-policy priorities through budget reconciliation.

events.title: Signs declaration supporting the Gaza peace agreement
events.summary: Trump joined the leaders of Egypt, Qatar and Turkey in a declaration backing implementation of an agreement intended to end the Gaza war and create a framework for security and reconstruction.

events.title: Appeals court vacates civil-fraud financial penalty
events.summary: A divided New York appellate court vacated the disgorgement awards as excessive while leaving the underlying fraud findings and other relief undisturbed; further appeal followed.
events.statusNote: New York's highest court had not supplied a final disposition in the sources checked for this review.

events.title: United States and Israel begin joint war against Iran
events.summary: Trump ordered major U.S. combat operations against Iran. The administration described goals including destroying missile capacity, naval forces and routes to a nuclear weapon; the war and its effects on shipping and energy remained active in October 2026.

events.title: Trump groups spend nearly $277 million on the midterms
events.summary: Associated Press reporting found that Trump's political groups had spent nearly $277 million late in the 2026 campaign to support Republican candidates, demonstrating his continued control over party resources while in office.

statements.summary: Trump presented “America First” as the organizing principle of his second administration.

statements.summary: Trump urged supporters to fight against certification of the election shortly before members of the crowd marched to the Capitol.

statements.summary: Trump described the federal prosecution of January 6 defendants as unjust while pardoning or commuting their sentences.

statements.summary: Trump used the constitutional language of invasion to justify restricting entry and access to asylum.

works.title: Trump: The Art of the Deal
works.detail: Credited to Donald Trump with Tony Schwartz; central to the dealmaker persona that preceded Trump's television and political careers.

chapters.title: From Queens to Manhattan
chapters.dek: A family real-estate business supplied the capital, relationships and operating structure for Trump's public career.
chapters.body:
Donald John Trump was born in Queens on June 14, 1946, the fourth of five children of Mary Anne MacLeod Trump and Fred Trump. Fred's company built and managed housing in Queens, Brooklyn and Staten Island. Donald attended New York Military Academy, began college at Fordham University, transferred to the University of Pennsylvania and graduated from its Wharton School in 1968. He then joined the family business full time. [[miller-life-brief, miller-before-presidency]]

Trump took control of the company in 1971 and renamed it the Trump Organization two years later. His early strategic move was geographic and social: he sought projects in Manhattan rather than remaining concentrated in the outer boroughs. The redevelopment of the Commodore Hotel as the Grand Hyatt depended on a long city tax abatement and a partnership with Hyatt, showing that public concessions, inherited connections and private financing were intertwined in the business from the beginning. [[miller-before-presidency]]

The Manhattan projects made Trump a public figure as well as a developer. Trump Tower, casinos and hotels put his name on the buildings themselves. That visibility became an asset independent of any one property, and it helped him survive financial setbacks that would have ended a less recognizable developer's public career. [[miller-before-presidency]]

chapters.title: The business became a brand
chapters.dek: Debt restructurings and casino bankruptcies coexisted with a growing image of wealth and command.
chapters.body:
Trump expanded into Atlantic City casinos during the 1980s, financing projects with substantial borrowing. The Taj Mahal entered bankruptcy protection in 1991 and the Trump Plaza Hotel followed in 1992. He subsequently used bankruptcy law to restructure company debts and placed casino holdings into a publicly traded company, while the privately held Trump Organization remained a collection of businesses principally or solely owned by him. [[miller-before-presidency]]

The setbacks did not end the image Trump had cultivated. The 1987 book Trump: The Art of the Deal presented him as a master negotiator, and the company increasingly licensed his name to properties and products. The distinction between the underlying businesses and the value of the Trump name became central: the public persona could generate fees and opportunity even when particular ventures struggled. [[miller-before-presidency]]

The Apprentice brought that persona into American homes beginning in 2004. Trump played a decisive executive who judged competitors and dismissed one each week with “You're fired.” The show and Celebrity Apprentice ran through 2015, creating a national audience that knew Trump less through real-estate records than through a staged version of business authority. [[miller-before-presidency]]

chapters.title: Celebrity became a political constituency
chapters.dek: Trump joined immigration, trade and national decline to a campaign built around his own capacity to act.
chapters.body:
Trump had floated presidential campaigns before 2015, including a Reform Party exploration in 1999. During Barack Obama's presidency he became a leading promoter of the false claim that Obama had not been born in the United States. That campaign placed Trump inside conservative media and activist politics before he held office and showed how he could keep an allegation in public circulation through repetition and celebrity. [[miller-campaigns]]

On June 16, 2015, Trump announced his Republican campaign at Trump Tower. He attacked existing immigration and trade policy, described the country as losing to foreign competitors and made “Make America Great Again” the campaign's organizing promise. The message fused a story of national decline with the dealmaker character developed through his books, licensing business and television work. [[miller-campaigns, miller-before-presidency]]

Trump defeated Hillary Clinton on November 8, 2016. The official count gave him 304 electoral votes to Clinton's 227, although Clinton led the national popular vote by about 2.9 million. The result made Trump the first president to enter office without prior public office or military leadership and turned a personal political brand into control of the executive branch. [[fec-2016-results, miller-life-brief]]

chapters.title: The first presidency
chapters.dek: Trump governed through the Republican Party while preserving the personal organization and communication style of his campaign.
chapters.body:
Trump took office as the 45th president on January 20, 2017. He transferred day-to-day management of the Trump Organization to his sons Donald Jr. and Eric but did not divest his ownership. Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner, joined the White House as advisers, keeping family members at the center of both the business and the administration and sustaining criticism that official decisions and private financial interests could overlap. [[miller-before-presidency, miller-life-brief]]

Immigration supplied the first test of presidential power. Trump's January 2017 entry order produced airport detentions, protests and immediate litigation; a revised proclamation restricted entry from several countries, most of them Muslim-majority, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2018. At the southwest border, the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance prosecution policy sharply increased the separation of children from parents before a federal court order and policy revision curtailed the practice. [[supreme-court-travel-ban, gao-family-separation, miller-domestic-affairs]]

With Republican congressional majorities, Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act in December 2017. It permanently cut the corporate tax rate to 21 percent and temporarily changed individual rates, credits and deductions. His administration also pursued broad deregulation and announced withdrawal from the Paris climate agreement, which Trump framed as protection of American workers and sovereignty. [[crs-2017-tax-law, miller-domestic-affairs, white-house-paris-2017]]

Appointments became one of the term's longest-lasting consequences. The Senate confirmed Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, giving Trump three lifetime appointments and moving the Court substantially to the right. His cabinet and White House, by contrast, experienced unusually high turnover as Trump repeatedly replaced senior officials who lost his confidence. [[senate-supreme-court-nominations, miller-domestic-affairs]]

The foreign-policy record mixed withdrawal with new agreements. Trump left the Paris accord and the Iran nuclear agreement, used tariffs as leverage against China and allies, and renegotiated NAFTA as the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which entered into force in July 2020. In September 2020 he hosted the Abraham Accords signing, which normalized relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. [[white-house-paris-2017, ustr-usmca, state-abraham-accords]]

Special counsel Robert Mueller documented extensive Russian efforts to influence the 2016 election and contacts involving Trump associates, but said the evidence was insufficient to charge a broader conspiracy. Mueller did not make a conventional prosecutorial judgment on whether Trump obstructed the investigation. Later in 2019 the House impeached Trump for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress after he pressed Ukraine's president to announce investigations affecting the 2020 campaign; the Senate acquitted him in February 2020. [[mueller-statement-2019, miller-life-brief, senate-impeachment-cases]]

chapters.title: The pandemic and the 2020 campaign
chapters.dek: COVID-19 brought the first presidency's deepest crisis, a rapid vaccine program and an election fought under emergency conditions.
chapters.body:
COVID-19 reached the United States in early 2020 and overtook public life in March. Trump declared a national emergency and signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act as states closed schools and businesses. He repeatedly minimized the danger in public, clashed with public-health officials and governors over reopening, and used racialized names for the virus while blaming China. By January 18, 2021, the reported U.S. death toll had passed 400,000. [[miller-domestic-affairs, cdc-covid-timeline]]

The administration also created Operation Warp Speed, a partnership of the health and defense departments that funded vaccine candidates and manufacturing before trial results were complete. By the end of Trump's term, the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines had received emergency authorization. The program was a major administrative success even as the initial distribution fell short of the administration's announced target. [[gao-warp-speed, cdc-covid-timeline]]

The emergency changed how Americans voted. Trump spent months attacking expanded mail voting and warning, without evidence, that fraud would be widespread. Election officials nevertheless certified Joe Biden's victory: 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232, with Biden ahead by about seven million votes nationally. [[fec-2020-results, january-6-report]]

Trump's refusal to accept that result turned the election from a campaign defeat into a constitutional crisis. Advisers, campaign lawyers and Justice Department officials told him that fraud claims were unsupported or insufficient to alter the result, but he continued to assert that he had won and began pressing officials who could affect certification. [[january-6-report, doj-smith-report-2025]]

chapters.title: Defeat, pressure and January 6
chapters.dek: The 2020 loss did not end Trump's leadership of the party; it produced an effort to reverse the certified result.
chapters.body:
Joe Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election, winning 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232 and leading the national popular vote by about seven million. Trump did not concede. He and his allies challenged results in court and pressed state and federal officials while publicly insisting that the election had been stolen. [[fec-2020-results, miller-life-brief]]

The House select committee that investigated January 6 later described a multi-part effort driven by Trump to overturn the result. Its report found that he spread false fraud claims after advisers told him they lacked evidence sufficient to change the outcome, pressed state officials, sought to use alternate electoral slates, urged the Justice Department to support his claims and pressured Vice President Mike Pence over the electoral count. These are the committee's findings; Trump rejected the investigation and its conclusions. [[january-6-report]]

On January 6, 2021, after Trump addressed supporters near the White House, members of the crowd marched to the Capitol and violently interrupted Congress's count of electoral votes. The House impeached him a second time. After Trump left office, the Senate tried and acquitted him on February 13, making him the first U.S. president impeached twice and the only former president returned to office after that history. [[january-6-report, senate-impeachment-cases, miller-life-brief]]

chapters.title: Legal jeopardy and political return
chapters.dek: Criminal and civil cases became part of Trump's campaign narrative rather than removing him from Republican leadership.
chapters.body:
Out of office, Trump remained the dominant Republican political figure. He continued telling supporters that the 2020 election had been stolen, endorsed candidates in Republican primaries and announced another presidential campaign while investigations of his conduct expanded. The party's institutions and electorate did not move on to a successor; challengers in the 2024 primary were forced to define themselves in relation to him. [[ap-2024-comeback, miller-campaigns]]

The prosecutions became part of Trump's campaign narrative. He described each case as political persecution and used court appearances to address supporters and news cameras. Rather than separating his legal defense from his campaign, he made the claim that both were one struggle against the same establishment. His Republican opponents largely rallied to him after indictments, narrowing the political cost of the cases inside the party. [[ap-2024-comeback]]

On July 13, 2024, a gunman opened fire during a Trump rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, grazing Trump's ear, killing attendee Corey Comperatore and seriously wounding two others. After Secret Service agents surrounded him, Trump rose with blood on his face, raised his fist and called “Fight.” The image became a campaign emblem two days before he appeared at the Republican convention. [[fbi-butler, ap-2024-comeback]]

Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris on November 5. The official results gave him 312 electoral votes to Harris's 226, and he won 49.8 percent of the national popular vote to Harris's 48.3 percent. The victory made him the second president, after Grover Cleveland, elected to nonconsecutive terms and showed that his movement could survive an election defeat, two impeachments, four criminal indictments, civil judgments and a felony conviction. [[fec-2024-results, miller-life-brief, ap-2024-comeback]]

chapters.title: The cases that followed him back to office
chapters.dek: Civil verdicts, criminal indictments and a felony conviction produced real judgments but did not prevent a second election victory.
chapters.body:
The legal cases arose from different conduct and ended in different procedural postures. In May 2023 a federal civil jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll and awarded $5 million. A second jury awarded $83.3 million in January 2024 for additional defamatory statements. Trump denied Carroll's account and appealed; the first judgment survived appellate review, while a Supreme Court petition concerning the larger award remained pending at the review cutoff. [[carroll-docket, carroll-83m-petition-2026]]

New York's attorney general separately pursued a civil case over financial statements used by the Trump Organization. The trial court found persistent fraud and imposed disgorgement and business restrictions in February 2024. In August 2025 a divided appellate court vacated the monetary awards as excessive but left the fraud findings undisturbed, and further appeal followed. [[ny-ag-fraud-judgment, ny-fraud-appeal-2025]]

Four criminal indictments were filed in 2023: a New York business-records case, federal and Georgia cases concerning the 2020 election, and a federal classified-documents case. The cases did not all reach trial. Special counsel Jack Smith dismissed the federal election prosecution after Trump's 2024 victory under Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president; the dismissal was not an acquittal or a verdict on the evidence. [[ap-2024-comeback, doj-smith-report-2025]]

The New York case did reach a jury. On May 30, 2024, Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records connected to reimbursements for a payment made before the 2016 election. In January 2025 the court imposed an unconditional discharge—no incarceration, fine or probation—so the conviction could become final for appeal before inauguration. Trump continued seeking to overturn it in 2026. [[manhattan-da-conviction, ny-courts-sentencing-order]]

At the same time, Trump Media & Technology Group became publicly traded, turning Truth Social into a large and volatile component of Trump's disclosed wealth. A December 2025 SEC filing reported 114.75 million shares—41.5 percent of the company—held by his revocable trust, with Donald Trump Jr. controlling voting and investment decisions as trustee and Trump remaining the sole beneficiary. [[sec-tmtg-ownership-2025]]

chapters.title: A second inauguration
chapters.dek: Trump returned with a stronger claim to party control and a promise to move quickly through executive power.
chapters.body:
Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge in the New York criminal case before taking office, leaving the conviction in place without jail, a fine, probation or community service while he pursued an appeal. On January 20, 2025, at age 78, he took the oath as the 47th president and became the oldest person inaugurated to the office. [[miller-life-brief, ny-courts-sentencing-order]]

His inaugural address described January 20 as “Liberation Day” and promised that every day of the administration would put “America first.” He announced immediate action on immigration, energy, the federal workforce, gender policy and other subjects, presenting his return not as a restoration of the first term but as authority to reverse the preceding administration quickly. [[white-house-inaugural-2025]]

chapters.title: A more concentrated second presidency
chapters.dek: Trump returned with tighter control of his party, a loyalty-tested administration and a broader theory of executive authority.
chapters.body:
The second administration was organized around people whose political standing depended more directly on Trump. JD Vance replaced Mike Pence as vice president; Susie Wiles, who managed the 2024 campaign, became chief of staff; and Stephen Miller returned as deputy chief of staff with broad responsibility for immigration policy. Family members did not hold the same formal White House posts they had in the first term, but Trump's political, business and family networks remained closely connected. [[white-house-administration-2026, white-house-staff-2026]]

Trump used the first day to erase symbols and consequences of his defeat. He pardoned nearly everyone convicted of offenses connected to January 6, commuted fourteen named sentences and ordered dismissal of pending cases. He also declared the southern border situation an “invasion,” restricted asylum access and directed agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from some children born in the United States, producing immediate constitutional challenges. [[white-house-j6-clemency-2025, white-house-border-2025, white-house-birthright-2025]]

The administration moved through executive orders to reduce the federal workforce, reverse environmental and diversity policies, expand immigration enforcement and use emergency authority for tariffs. Congress supplied its central legislative vehicle on July 4, 2025, when Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, extending core provisions of the 2017 tax law and financing border, energy and social-policy priorities. The administration celebrated the law as fulfillment of campaign promises; its distributional and fiscal effects require the independent quantitative treatment kept outside that claim. [[white-house-obbba-2025, ap-economy-2026]]

Foreign policy moved from campaign promises to end wars toward greater direct use of American power. Trump backed an October 2025 agreement intended to end the Gaza war and signed a declaration with Egypt, Qatar and Turkey supporting its implementation. On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel began joint strikes against Iran. Trump said the American objectives were to destroy Iranian missile capacity and naval forces and prevent a nuclear weapon; by October the war and conflict around the Strait of Hormuz remained active and were contributing to higher energy prices. [[white-house-gaza-2025, white-house-iran-2026, ap-iran-war-2026, ap-economy-2026]]

Trump's control of Republican resources remained a separate source of power from formal office. By October 21, 2026, his political groups had spent nearly $277 million in a late push for Republican midterm candidates, an extraordinary intervention by a sitting president's organizations. The spending tied congressional careers to Trump's fundraising network while the election became a referendum on tariffs, immigration, prices and the Iran war. [[ap-midterms-spending-2026, ap-economy-2026]]

The second presidency is still an active record. Its defining pattern through October 22, 2026 is the conversion of personal political authority into control over appointments, party money and aggressive assertions of executive power. Some actions produced durable law; others remained in litigation or depended on emergency powers. The profile therefore records outcomes separately from announcements and leaves unresolved cases marked as such. [[white-house-staff-2026, white-house-obbba-2025, ap-midterms-spending-2026]]
